content: There is no level of lead in the blood that is considered safe for children. Even minimal exposure to lead can result in harmful health effects. Young children are particularly vulnerable to lead exposure because they often engage in hand-to-mouth behaviors, such as putting toys, dirt, or other objects into their mouths. This increases the likelihood of ingesting lead dust. Lead is a naturally occurring metal, but it is toxic to humans. Exposure to lead can occur through various routes, including consuming lead-contaminated food or water, inhaling lead dust, or ingesting lead-based paint chips. Children under the age of six are at the highest risk of lead exposure due to their developmental behaviors and increased absorption of lead compared to adults. No blood lead level (BLL) in children has been identified as safe. Even low levels of lead in the blood are linked to developmental delays, learning difficulties, and behavioral problems. The damage caused by lead poisoning can be permanent and may result in long-term disabilities. Parents and healthcare providers can take proactive measures to protect children from lead exposure. If there is a concern that a child has been exposed to lead, healthcare providers can perform a blood lead test to assess the level of lead in the child’s blood. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has established a blood lead reference value (BLRV) of 3.5 micrograms per deciliter (µg/dL). This reference value is used to identify children whose blood lead levels are higher than those of most children. It is estimated that approximately 500,000 children in the United States have blood lead levels at or above the BLRV. Healthcare providers can refer to the CDC’s Recommended Actions Based on Blood Lead Level to create a tailored plan of care for children with elevated blood lead levels. Children may be exposed to lead from various sources, including lead-based paint, contaminated water, soil, certain imported products, and industrial emissions. Additionally, children can be exposed indirectly through their parents or caregivers who may bring lead home from certain occupations or hobbies. Lead exposure can occur in environments where children live, learn, and play.
